explanations: luna: The section's dictionary gloss calls the learned teacher one who feeds people small sciences; this ayah shows Allah teaching Adam the names, a foundational act of instruction.
luna: The section says mercy becomes good treatment, especially for the weak and kin; this ayah joins goodness to parents and relatives with care for orphans and the needy.
luna: The section extends upbringing into teaching; Abraham asks for a messenger who will recite signs and teach the Book and wisdom to his descendants.
terra: Abraham and Jacob charge their sons with a durable religious inheritance, a parental form of cultivation beyond bodily upbringing.
terra: Jacob asks his sons what they will worship after him, and their answer displays the fruit of intergenerational teaching at the edge of his death.
luna: The section describes teaching as a form of nurture; this ayah says the Messenger recites, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom to the community.

luna: The section connects kinship to practical care; this ayah includes spending on relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler among acts of righteousness. | terra: Righteousness gives cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, specifying mercy as costly beneficence rather than feeling alone.

luna: The section makes care for family and the vulnerable an expression of goodness; this ayah names parents, near relatives, orphans, and the needy as recipients of spending. | terra: When asked what to spend, the ayah names parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy; provision follows the family-and-weakness network of the section.

luna: The section includes a child raised by someone other than a birth parent; this ayah says improving orphans' affairs is best and describes them as brothers when their lives are joined. | terra: “Improvement for them is best” makes orphan care an active good, and calling them brothers prevents guardianship from becoming exploitation.

luna: The section moves from the womb into nurture at home; this ayah sets nursing and weaning, forbids harming either parent through the child, and assigns the child's father provision and clothing for the nursing mother. | terra: Mothers nurse for two complete years, while the father supplies food and clothing; it gives the section's house, duration, nourishment, and completion concrete legal form.

luna: The section makes the womb a house where the child is formed; this ayah says Allah shapes people in the wombs (ٱلْأَرْحَامِ), making that hidden home an act of divine formation. | terra: God fashions people “فِي الْأَرْحَامِ” as He wills, making the womb the place of divine formation described by the section.

luna: The section treats the womb as a child's home; Mary's mother dedicates what is in her womb, making the unborn child the center of a household vow. | terra: The wife of ʿImran dedicates what is in her womb before birth, treating the unborn child as already held in a divine and familial trust.

luna: The section moves from womb to the child's later life; this ayah records Mary's birth and her mother's naming her, carrying the image from gestation into family care. | terra: At Mary's birth her mother names her and seeks protection for her and her descendants, extending maternal care into prayerful safeguarding.

luna: The section says a child can be raised by someone other than the one who gave birth; this ayah says Zakariyya took charge of Mary (كَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا) and that she grew under his care. | terra: Mary is accepted, made to grow a good growth, and placed in Zakariyya's care; this is Qur'anic tarbiya as gradual growth under a guardian.

luna: The section explicitly links its dictionary sense of rabb as a teacher who feeds people small units of knowledge to rabbāniyyūn; this ayah says to be rabbāniyyūn through teaching the Book. | terra: “رَبَّانِيِّينَ” is tied to teaching and studying the Book, explicitly extending Rabb-root nurture into the work of a teacher.

luna: The section defines raḥmah as a tenderness that leads to good treatment; this ayah says the Prophet was gentle with people by Allah's mercy. | terra: Mercy from God makes the Prophet gentle with people; the verse makes raḥma a tenderness that produces a concrete way of treating others.
luna: The section makes teaching part of nurture; this ayah says the Messenger recites, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom to the believers.

luna: The section says kin are named through the womb because they came from one womb; this ayah joins reverence for Allah with care for ٱلْأَرْحَامِ, making the bodily origin a social bond. | terra: The command to fear God explicitly names “الْأَرْحَامَ”; kinship is held together with the womb word from which the section derives its social sense.

luna: The section's household image centers on sustaining a vulnerable child; this ayah forbids guardians from consuming or exchanging orphans' property, marking a boundary against exploiting those in their care. | terra: The command to give orphans their property and not consume it with one's own makes material integrity part of care for the weak.
terra: Fear of failing to deal justly with orphans is made a threshold for the marriage ruling; it keeps the weak dependent's right in view within household formation.

luna: The section's dictionary form qiwām describes what keeps a household standing; this ayah calls wealth قِيَامًا لِّلنَّاسِ and immediately orders provision and clothing for dependents. | terra: Property is called a means of qiyām and guardians must provide food, clothing, and kind speech to dependents; it is the household-support sense named for qiwām.

luna: The section defines upbringing as carrying someone to completion; this ayah orders guardians to test orphans until they reach marriageable maturity and then return their property, specifying care up to adulthood. | terra: Guardians test orphans until marriageable age and sound judgment before returning their property, making care answerable to a child's gradual maturity.

luna: The section describes a household's care and provision for relatives and vulnerable people; this ayah instructs that relatives, orphans, and the needy present at an inheritance division receive something from it. | terra: When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend a division, they are to receive provision and kind speech, carrying household resources outward to the weak.

luna: The section's image makes adults responsible for the vulnerable child; this ayah warns people to fear leaving behind weak offspring and to speak rightly about them. | terra: It warns people to fear leaving weak offspring behind; the imagined vulnerable children make responsible speech and provision a present duty.
terra: Consuming orphan property unjustly is described as consuming fire; it is the direct opposite of the patient guardianship required for a vulnerable child.

luna: The section's listed dictionary form rabība means a girl cared for by a step-parent; this ayah names الرَّبَائِبُ and locates them in the household's حجر, the very family setting the image develops. | terra: “رَبَائِبُكُمُ ... فِي حُجُورِكُمْ” names stepdaughters in one's care, directly matching the section's non-birth parent who assumes upbringing.

luna: The section links al-mustaqīm's root q-w-m to qiwām, the one who sustains a household; this ayah calls men قَوَّامُونَ over women and connects that role to spending from their wealth. | terra: The term قَوَّامُونَ is joined to spending from wealth and guarding the unseen, supplying the house-sustaining responsibility developed from the section's qiwām sense.

luna: The section describes mercy as practical goodness toward relatives and the weak; this ayah commands ihsan to parents, kin, orphans, and the needy. | terra: Goodness to parents, kin, orphans, and needy neighbors maps a widening household of vulnerable relations that calls for ihsan.
terra: The ruling explicitly concerns orphan girls and weak children and commands justice for orphans, extending guardianship to those structurally least able to protect themselves.
terra: The rabbāniyyūn are entrusted to guard the Book and bear witness to it; the named derivative joins learning with custodial responsibility.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of rabb as a teacher who nourishes people with knowledge has an ethical boundary here: rabbāniyyūn and scholars are rebuked for not forbidding wrongdoing. | terra: The rabbāniyyūn are blamed for failing to restrain sinful speech and consumption; the named teacher-caretaker role is shown by its neglected duty.
terra: Jesus is taught scripture and wisdom and speaks to people in the cradle and in maturity; teaching and a life-span of formation are held in one address.
terra: Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision are declared lost; the ayah fuses harm to children with denial of sustenance.

luna: The section presents care as protection and provision for the vulnerable child; this ayah forbids killing children for poverty and says Allah provides for them and their parents. | terra: The command not to kill children from poverty is joined to “We provide for you and them,” reversing fear-driven refusal of the child's provision.
terra: Orphan property may be approached only in the best manner until maturity, matching stewardship that lasts through a child's growth.

luna: The section follows the child from the womb into a family that cares for it; this ayah moves from pregnancy to birth and the parents' prayer for a sound child. | terra: A wife carries a light burden which becomes heavy, making pregnancy itself a scene of shared human dependence and appeal to God.

luna: The section explains kinship through people emerging from one womb; this ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another in Allah's decree. | terra: “أُولُو الْأَرْحَامِ” are closer to one another by God's ordinance, giving legal force to the claim that kin share a womb-origin.
luna: The section says a teacher feeds people small units of knowledge; this ayah describes some believers studying religion so they can warn and teach their people when they return.

luna: The section makes mercy a response to another's hardship; this ayah says the Messenger is distressed by believers' suffering and is compassionate and merciful toward them. | terra: The Messenger is grieved by believers' hardship and is “رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ” toward them, giving the mercy-name an attentive, protective stance.
terra: Noah calls his son to board the ark and avoid the unbelievers; parental protection appears as an urgent invitation to safety.
terra: Noah pleads that his son belongs to his family, making biological and household kinship the explicit ground of his appeal.
terra: Answering Noah's plea in 11:45, God says the son is not of his family because of unrighteous conduct; it marks a boundary where biological kinship alone does not secure the familial claim.
terra: In the annunciation to Sarah, God's mercy and blessing are spoken over “people of the house”; birth promise, house, and raḥma meet explicitly.
terra: Jacob warns his son Joseph not to disclose the vision to his brothers, a father's specific effort to protect a child's vulnerable future within a divided household.
terra: Joseph's Rabb will teach him interpretation and complete His favor upon him and Jacob's family, joining education, divine lordship, and a family-wide niʿma.
terra: The Egyptian purchaser tells his wife to honor Joseph's lodging and considers taking him as a son; this is a direct non-biological household receiving and raising a child.
terra: When Joseph reaches full strength, God gives him judgment and knowledge, a second child-to-maturity sequence alongside Moses' growth in 28:14.
terra: Jacob calls God the best guardian and the most merciful, binding protection of a child-like dependent to the divine mercy named by the section.

luna: The section's dictionary note gives a secondary sense of ghayra as provisions brought home; the brothers say نَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا, that they will procure provisions for their family. | terra: The brothers promise both “we will provision our family” and “guard our brother”; its paired acts closely realize the source's secondary senses of household provision and protective care.

luna: The section says the womb is where Allah shapes a child as He wills; this ayah says Allah knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, placing development under measured knowledge. | terra: God knows what every womb carries and its decrease and increase, with everything measured; hidden gestation is both known and ordered.
luna: The section presents kinship as a bond issuing from one womb; this ayah condemns breaking the covenant and the ties Allah commanded to be joined.

luna: The section's womb-and-house image includes feeding and sheltering a child; Abraham leaves some descendants in a barren valley and asks Allah to provide fruit for them and turn hearts toward them. | terra: Abraham settles descendants by the Sacred House and asks for provision of fruits; a parent locates children within worship and material sustenance.
terra: The man given news of a daughter darkens and suppresses grief, a social reversal of receiving a newborn as a mercy and trust.
terra: His deliberation whether to keep the daughter in humiliation or bury her exposes the cruel opposite of sheltering and raising the weak.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss describes a newly delivered ewe kept at home for milk; this ayah describes milk produced by livestock, a concrete parallel to the household's animal nourishment. | terra: Milk from cattle is a pure drink from within their bodies, activating the section's sheep-kept-for-milk sense as nourishment supplied through living creatures.

luna: The section links a household with children and its material sustenance; this ayah says Allah made spouses, sons, and grandchildren for people and provided good things. | terra: God makes spouses, children, and grandchildren, then provides good things; family generation and household provision are named together.

luna: The section frames the womb as the first home before a child's later upbringing; this ayah says people are brought out of their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts. | terra: Humans emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts, joining birth to the beginning of learning.

luna: The section says mercy becomes ihsan, especially toward the weak; this ayah commands justice and ihsan and names giving to close kin. | terra: The command for justice, ihsan, and giving to near kin gives Qur'anic form to the section's definition of mercy as tenderness that becomes beneficence.

luna: The section brings the word Rabb into a family setting; this ayah begins the command to worship Allah alone and show ihsan to one's parents. | terra: The Rabb's command joins exclusive worship to ihsan toward parents, putting family care inside the Lord's ordering of a home.

luna: The section's roots are joined in this prayer: the source's dictionary form raḥmah appears in ٱرْحَمْهُمَا, and its child-rearing sense of rabb appears in رَبَّيَانِي; grown children ask care for the parents who raised them. | terra: The child answers parental raising with mercy: “رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا” explicitly joins Rabb, raḥma, and being raised while small.

luna: The section says kinship grows from a shared womb and calls for care; this ayah commands giving close relatives their due, along with the needy and traveler. | terra: Giving the near relative his due, along with the needy and traveler, turns kinship into concrete household-like provision.

luna: The section's home carries a duty to feed and protect the child; this ayah forbids killing children from poverty and says Allah provides for both parents and children. | terra: The same prohibition addresses fear of impoverishment and promises provision for children and parents, setting divine sustenance against parental desperation.
terra: The same protection of orphan property “until he reaches maturity” makes legal restraint an expression of long-term care.
luna: The section's teacher nourishes learners through small portions; this ayah says the Qur'an was divided so it could be recited to people over intervals.
terra: God gives His servant mercy and teaches him knowledge from Himself; the verse directly joins raḥma and instruction, the meeting the section develops through the teacher.
luna: The section extends rabb's upbringing sense to teaching; this ayah shows Moses asking Khidr to teach him from the knowledge Allah had given Khidr.

luna: The section presents a child's home as a place of nurture; this ayah gives a difficult boundary in the Moses-and-Khidr account, where the boy's future conduct is feared to burden his believing parents. | terra: The boy's believing parents are feared to be burdened by his rebellion and disbelief, a hard case in which parent-child welfare is judged beyond ordinary visible care.

luna: After 18:80 explains the feared harm to the parents, this ayah states the hope that their Lord replace the boy with one better in purity and nearer to affection, framing a severe act as protection for the family. | terra: Following 18:80, the stated replacement is a child better in purity and nearer in mercy for the parents; its own contribution is the mercy-oriented outcome of that difficult boundary case.

luna: The section presents a household that shelters and raises a child; this ayah protects the treasure of two orphan boys until they reach strength, explaining the shelter through their righteous father. | terra: The wall preserves treasure for two orphan boys until they reach maturity, explicitly calling this delayed protection a mercy from their Lord.

luna: The section extends upbringing into learning; this ayah tells Yahya to take the Scripture firmly while still a child. | terra: John receives judgment while still a child, showing divine formation can include early moral and intellectual capacity.

luna: The section defines raḥmah as tenderness leading to good; this ayah describes Yahya as receiving tenderness (حَنَانًا) and purity from Allah. | terra: John receives tenderness from God along with purity and piety, a spiritual counterpart to compassion shaping a child.

luna: The section joins the child's upbringing to later care for parents; this ayah says Yahya was dutiful to his parents and not arrogant or rebellious. | terra: John is devoted to his parents and not arrogant or disobedient, presenting filial character as an outcome of formed life.
terra: Jesus' birth is announced as a sign and a mercy from God, linking an extraordinary childbearing scene to mercy made manifest.

luna: The section follows the child from the womb into a life outside it; this ayah says Mary conceived and withdrew with him, giving a concrete mother-and-child scene. | terra: Mary conceives and withdraws with the child to a distant place, staging pregnancy as a sheltered but exposed maternal passage.

luna: The section's dictionary note describes a mother animal suffering in her womb after giving birth; this ayah gives the human parallel of Mary's labor pain, specifically linking birth to bodily cost. | terra: Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk, a direct birth scene that gives bodily cost to the commentary's maternal image.

luna: The section presents care as meeting a vulnerable mother and child; in the immediate birth scene this ayah answers Mary's distress with reassurance and a stream beneath her. | terra: At childbirth she is told not to grieve and is provided a stream; divine mercy appears as immediate care for a vulnerable mother.

luna: The section's house image includes provision for a growing child; this ayah tells Mary to shake the palm trunk so fresh dates fall for her after labor. | terra: Fresh dates are provided through the palm, turning provision into bodily support during the birth scene.

luna: The section joins maternal care with the child's home; this ayah tells Mary to eat, drink, and be comforted after delivery. | terra: “Eat, drink, and be comforted” completes the care of Mary after delivery rather than leaving mercy as an abstraction.
terra: Jesus declares himself devoted to his mother and not made arrogant or wretched, giving the child-side response to parental mercy a distinct formulation.
terra: Ishmael commands his family to prayer and almsgiving, making care for a household include formed habits of worship and generosity.

luna: The section uses Moses' infancy to show divine care working through his mother; this ayah recalls Allah inspiring Moses' mother before the rescue by the river. | terra: This ayah identifies Moses' mother as the recipient of divine inspiration; 20:39 gives the instruction itself, while 20:38 supplies its maternal beginning.

luna: The section says the child is raised under the Lord's care; this ayah recounts placing Moses in the chest and says he was brought up under Allah's eye (عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي). | terra: God directs Moses' passage from mother to river to Pharaoh's house so that he may be brought up under God's eye; the true rearer exceeds the visible household.

luna: The section follows Moses through separation, reunion, and growth; this ayah recalls his sister's intervention, his return to his mother, and his reaching maturity. | terra: The sister's intervention returns Moses to his mother for her comfort; this ayah supplies the reunion and maternal relief following 20:39.
terra: Moses defines the Rabb as the one who gives every thing its creation and then guides it, a concise cosmic analogue to formation toward its proper end.
luna: The section's teacher develops learners gradually; this ayah tells the Prophet not to hasten ahead of revelation and to ask, رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا, for increased knowledge.

luna: The section says a household's affairs are kept standing by its sustainer; this ayah commands the Prophet to enjoin prayer on his family and says, نَحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ, that Allah provides. | terra: The addressee is told to command his family to prayer and persevere, while God—not the caretaker—guarantees provision; spiritual care and sustenance meet.

luna: The section says the womb is where Allah forms a child as He wills; this ayah says Mary guarded her chastity and Allah made her and her son a sign, placing divine care in a specific mother-and-child story.
terra: At the Hour, every nursing mother is distracted from the child she nursed and every pregnant woman delivers her burden; the catastrophe reverses ordinary maternal holding and care.

luna: The section describes a child being brought along toward completion; this ayah moves from drop to formed and unformed lump, then birth and maturity, making growth in stages explicit. | terra: It explicitly traces embryonic stages, remaining in wombs for an appointed term, infancy, and maturity; the whole arc is the section's place-and-time growth.
luna: The section begins with the womb as the child's place of origin; this ayah traces human creation from an extract of clay toward the later stages of gestation.

luna: The section calls the womb a house and vessel; this ayah places the drop in a secure resting-place (قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ), directly extending the image of protected lodging. | terra: The drop is put in a secure resting-place, a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the womb as a child's enclosing home.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss defines tarbiya as taking something state by state to completion; this ayah names successive bodily transformations and then a further creation. | terra: The passage moves the embryo through distinct states until another creation, directly realizing tarbiya as being brought state by state toward completion.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss makes milk from a lactating ewe part of household provision; this ayah points to livestock as a source of drink and food. | terra: Cattle provide drink from what is in their bellies and other benefits; it makes animal milk a sign of provision rather than merely an animal fact.
luna: The section's dictionary note includes children raised in comfort; this ayah questions whether wealth and children are being mistaken for good things hurried by Allah.
luna: The section notes the luxury sense in raising children; this ayah completes the warning that wealth and children do not prove that Allah is hastening good for their owners.
luna: The section joins mercy with kinship care; this ayah tells those with means not to withhold from relatives and the poor, but to pardon and overlook.
terra: Children who have not reached puberty learn three household privacy times; the home protects them while teaching boundaries appropriate to their stage.
terra: When children reach puberty they seek permission like adults, marking a concrete transition from one state of household formation to another.
luna: The section describes development state by state; this ayah explains that the Qur'an came in stages to strengthen the Prophet's heart and be recited distinctly.
terra: God creates the human from water and makes bonds of blood relation and marriage; it broadens the womb-derived kinship image to the family ties that make a household.

luna: The section describes family care that helps a child grow toward completion; this prayer asks for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes and for the family to lead the mindful. | terra: The prayer for spouses and descendants to be comfort of the eyes makes a flourishing household an object of responsible hope.

luna: The section calls Pharaoh's upbringing claim incomplete; Pharaoh says he raised Moses among his household as a child, giving the claim the exact words the section qualifies. | terra: Pharaoh says “نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا”; against the prior maternal nursing and divine watchfulness, his claim to have raised Moses is deliberately incomplete.
luna: After Pharaoh's upbringing claim in 26:18, this ayah supplies his accusation against Moses; it shows the palace's account of care is immediately framed as a grievance and charge of ingratitude.
luna: The section's Moses image shows a child protected and raised; this ayah supplies the danger around his infancy, as Pharaoh oppressed the people and slaughtered their sons.
luna: The section says mercy attends a vulnerable child; this ayah says Allah intended to favor those oppressed in the land and make them leaders and inheritors.

luna: After 28:5 states favor for the oppressed, this ayah says Allah would establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and his people what they feared, completing the reversal of Pharaoh's power over Moses' family.

luna: The section uses Moses' infancy to show care continuing after birth; this ayah commands his mother to nurse him and, when afraid, place him in the river. | terra: Moses' mother is commanded to nurse him, then entrust him amid danger; it makes maternal feeding and fear part of the child's first care.

luna: The section's child leaves his mother's home and is taken into another household; this ayah says Pharaoh's people picked Moses up, setting the foster-household scene in motion. | terra: Pharaoh's family picks Moses up only for him to become an enemy and grief to them; before 28:9 proposes adoption, this ayah makes the foster household a dangerous reversal.

luna: The section describes another household's care for Moses; Pharaoh's wife calls him an eye's delight for herself and her husband and asks that he not be killed. | terra: Pharaoh's wife proposes that the found child may be a comfort or be taken as a son, opening the question of a home beyond biological parentage.

luna: The section names the separation between mother and child; this ayah says Moses' mother's heart became empty, showing the cost of the child's removal. | terra: The mother's heart becomes empty after separation, showing the wound left when the child leaves the maternal enclosure.

luna: The section follows a family trying to protect a child from afar; this ayah says Moses' sister watched him from a distance while they did not recognize her. | terra: Moses' sister is told to follow him and keeps watch from a distance; her own act is sibling vigilance during the child's transfer between households.

luna: The section's dictionary form rāb/rābba means a spouse who takes up a child's upbringing; this ayah offers Pharaoh's household a family who will nurse and care for Moses. | terra: Moses refuses other nurses, and his sister offers a household that will take charge of him; nursing, foster care, and a house meet in one ayah.

luna: The section says the child returns from another household to his mother; this ayah says Allah returned Moses to her so her eye would be comforted. | terra: Moses is returned to his mother so that her eye may be comforted and she not grieve; care restores the broken mother-child bond.

luna: The section defines tarbiya as carrying something state by state to completion; this ayah marks Moses reaching maturity and receiving judgment and knowledge. | terra: On reaching full strength and maturity Moses receives judgment and knowledge, giving an end point to the childhood-care sequence.

luna: The section links a mother's bodily labor with a child's upbringing and care; this ayah commands goodness to parents and recalls the mother's hardship in carrying and weaning. | terra: People are enjoined to goodness toward parents, while obedience has a boundary when they press toward association; it parallels the qualified filial kindness of 31:15.

luna: The section defines raḥmah as tenderness that leads to good treatment; this ayah places affection and mercy between spouses, locating that care within a household. | terra: Affection and “رَحْمَةً” are placed between spouses; this supplies the relational mercy in which a family home and later child care can exist.
terra: The near relative, needy, and traveler receive their due; the ayah makes generous support the better path for those seeking God.
luna: The section defines upbringing as bringing something through states toward completion; this ayah traces human life from weakness to strength and then weakness and old age.

luna: The section connects child-rearing with instruction; Luqman begins addressing his son with foundational guidance against associating partners with Allah. | terra: Luqman's address “my son” begins parental teaching with a specific moral boundary against associating partners with God.

luna: The section makes the womb and later upbringing one continuum; this ayah names a mother's strain in carrying and weaning her child, then commands gratitude to parents. | terra: The mother carries weakness upon weakness and weans over two years, grounding filial gratitude in bodily, gradual maternal care.

luna: The section places upbringing within a family relation; this ayah tells a child to remain companionably kind to parents even when refusing their demand to associate partners with Allah. | terra: Even where parents press toward wrong, the child must accompany them with kindness in this world; filial mercy has a moral boundary without becoming abandonment.

luna: The section's teacher develops a child's understanding; Luqman teaches his son that even a tiny deed hidden in a rock or the heavens or earth is known to Allah. | terra: Luqman teaches his son through the mustard-seed image, an example of giving moral knowledge in a small, graspable form.

luna: The section extends rabb's care into teaching; Luqman instructs his son in prayer, good conduct, and patience. | terra: The father gives his son a sequence of practices—prayer, right action, resistance to wrong, patience—showing formation through teachable acts.

luna: The section depicts upbringing as preparing a child for life among others; Luqman teaches his son not to turn away from people or walk arrogantly. | terra: The instruction against contempt and arrogant walking makes character formation part of parental teaching.

luna: The section describes education as developing capacities over time; Luqman gives his son practical counsel on his pace and voice. | terra: Moderating one's walk and voice continues the father's detailed, gradual education of his child.
terra: Knowledge of what is in wombs belongs to God, preserving the womb as both a real home and a hidden domain beyond human command.
terra: After proportioning the human, God gives spirit, hearing, sight, and hearts; bodily formation opens into capacities for perception and learning.

luna: The section includes step-parents who raise a child; this ayah distinguishes adopted sons from biological sons, clarifying that care and lineage are related but not identical. | terra: God says adopted sons are not one's actual sons; the legal boundary clarifies the section's distinction between biological origin and the person who raises a child.

luna: The section allows a child to be raised by someone other than a birth parent; this ayah says adopted children should be called by their fathers when known, preserving lineage within that care. | terra: Calling adopted children by their fathers preserves lineage, while the verse still calls them brothers and clients when parentage is unknown; care survives a boundary of descent.

luna: The section explains kinship through people emerging from one womb; this ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another in Allah's Book, giving that tie a practical priority. | terra: The verse again makes those of the arḥām closer in God's Book, distinguishing durable kin obligation from looser social affiliation.
terra: No female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge, explicitly placing pregnancy and delivery under divine care.
terra: In the cattle passage, people have benefits and drinks from the animals; this repeats the domestic nourishment activated by the sheep-kept-for-milk detail.
terra: Abraham asks his Lord for a righteous child; the prayer makes offspring a hoped-for trust before the good news and later maturity in 37:101–102.
terra: The answer is glad tidings of a forbearing boy, giving the desired child an ethically formed quality before the father-son scene of 37:102.
terra: When the promised son reaches the age to work with Abraham, father and son deliberate together; maturity appears as shared responsibility within a parent-child bond.

luna: The section calls the womb a child's house and vessel; this ayah places creation within three layers of darkness in the womb, giving that shelter a concrete bodily setting. | terra: “Creation after creation” in mothers' wombs makes the womb a hidden dwelling of successive formation rather than a single moment.

luna: The section describes growth from one state to another until completion; this ayah traces creation through drop, clot, infant, maturity, and old age. | terra: The ayah runs from reproductive origin through childhood and full strength to old age, an extended Qur'anic sequence of human growth.
terra: No female conceives or gives birth outside God's knowledge; in an eschatological setting it repeats the hidden maternal scene as a limit on human knowledge.
luna: The section says Allah shapes the child in the womb as He wills; this ayah says Allah gives daughters or sons as He wills, placing a child's sex within divine choice.
luna: The section's womb image is a home for a child being formed; this ayah supplies the boundary case of barrenness, where no child is granted.

luna: The section links womb, birth, and raising a child; this ayah names the mother's hardship in pregnancy and delivery, the full gestation-and-weaning term, and a prayer for righteous descendants. | terra: Pregnancy and birth come with hardship, followed by weaning and full strength; it includes the mother's cost that the she-camel dictionary sense keeps visible.

luna: The section explains kinship through the womb; this ayah names cutting the womb-ties (تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ) as the opposite of honoring that bond. | terra: Turning away is described as spreading corruption and severing “أَرْحَامَكُمْ,” reversing the womb-derived bond the section treats as a claim of care.

luna: After 47:22 names cutting womb-ties, this ayah gives the consequence of that rupture: divine curse and loss of sight and hearing. | terra: Following 47:22's severing of kinship ties, this ayah names God's curse and loss of hearing and sight; it supplies the consequence of that rupture.
luna: The section extends tenderness into a bond between people; this ayah describes the believers as merciful toward one another (رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ).
terra: God knows people best while they are hidden embryos in their mothers' wombs; hidden origin becomes a reason not to declare oneself pure.

luna: The section develops Rahman as a teacher; this ayah names ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ, whose teaching of the Qur'an is stated in 55:2. | terra: “الرَّحْمَٰنُ” names the merciful source of the teaching and human-creation sequence in 55:2–4; its own contribution is the teacher's merciful identity.

luna: The section says a teacher feeds learners small portions of knowledge; this ayah gives the Rahman the direct act عَلَّمَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ, teaching the Qur'an. | terra: The Merciful teaches the Qur'an, making instruction itself an act of raḥma rather than a detached transfer of information.

luna: The section joins nurture and creation in the image of a child growing; this ayah places creation of the human between the Rahman's teaching of Qur'an and teaching of expression. | terra: Human creation follows the teaching of the Qur'an, keeping formation and instruction together in the section's order.

luna: The section's teacher develops the learner's capacities; this ayah says the human was taught البيان, the ability to express and make clear. | terra: Teaching human beings clear expression brings the growing creature into communicative maturity.

luna: The section distinguishes the womb from later care by another adult; this ayah sets the boundary that a man's wife does not become his mother by speech, and says mothers are those who gave birth.
luna: The section's image extends care into instruction; this ayah repeats the sequence of recitation, purification, and teaching the Book and wisdom.

luna: The section pictures the household as a place of care and protection; this ayah marks a boundary by warning that some spouses and children may oppose a believer, while commanding pardon and forbearance.
luna: The section notes children raised in comfort; this ayah warns that wealth and children are a trial, limiting any assumption that household provision itself proves spiritual good.

luna: The section moves from womb to home care; this ayah orders housing for divorced mothers, spending during pregnancy, and payment or consultation over nursing the child. | terra: It orders housing and provision for a pregnant mother, payment for nursing, and another nurse if needed: care can be shared without abandoning the child.

luna: The section's secondary gloss of ghayra evokes protecting one's household; this ayah directly commands believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire. | terra: “Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire” turns guarding the household into a responsibility that includes its ultimate safety.

luna: The section follows a child from the womb through formation; this ayah recalls the human beginning as a drop of emitted fluid. | terra: The emitted drop recalls the first, dependent state before the later making and proportioning in the next ayat.

luna: The section describes growth state by state; this ayah names the next stage, the drop becoming a clinging form. | terra: The drop becomes a clinging form, preserving the section's attention to distinct formative stages.

luna: The section's image makes divine formation in the womb perceptible; this ayah says Allah formed and proportioned the human and made from him male and female. | terra: God makes and proportionates, then differentiates male and female; formation is purposeful rather than merely biological.
terra: The human is created from a mixed drop and given hearing and sight; physical origin is immediately linked to capacities through which learning and testing occur.

luna: The section defines raḥmah as doing good to the one shown mercy, especially the weak; this ayah depicts feeding the needy, orphan, and captive out of love for Allah. | terra: Those who feed food despite loving it give it to the needy, orphan, and captive; mercy is enacted through nourishment of the vulnerable.
terra: Human origin from a weak fluid begins the sequence whose protected place and measured term follow in this passage.

luna: The section presents the womb as a house for the growing child; this ayah calls the embryo's place a secure repository (قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ), giving the shelter image a direct parallel. | terra: The fluid is placed in a “firm resting-place,” a particularly close parallel to the womb as container and house.

luna: The section's upbringing proceeds toward completion over time; this ayah says the embryo remains there until a known term (قَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ). | terra: Its “known measure” supplies the duration within which the section says mercy and growth work.

luna: The section says care carries a thing through stages to its limit; this ayah names divine measuring and determining in the embryo's development. | terra: God's determining completes the preceding protected-place image: formation has a measure and an active determiner.
luna: The section takes the child from an enclosed beginning toward completion; this ayah asks what the human was created from, opening a passage about formation.

luna: The section makes the womb the first home of a growing child; this ayah says the human was created from a drop and then measured. | terra: From a drop God creates and determines the human, linking dependence at origin with measured formation.

luna: The section describes care as carrying a child from one state to another; this ayah says Allah made the human's path easy after creation. | terra: God then makes the way easy, extending determination into guided movement through life.
terra: The buried girl is summoned to speak, bringing the most vulnerable child into judgment rather than leaving her outside protection.
terra: The question “for what sin was she killed?” condemns the destruction of a daughter where the section sees the child as someone to nurture.
terra: The human is addressed before “your generous Rabb,” so bodily formation is framed as a gift from the nurturing Lord rather than self-production.
terra: God creates, proportions, and balances the human, a compact account of being made fit stage by stage.
terra: God composes the human in whatever form He wills, echoing the form-giving in wombs without repeating its setting.
luna: The section defines tarbiya as moving something state by state; this ayah says people will pass from one state to another, extending that staged-life image beyond childhood.
terra: The Creator both makes and proportions; its paired verbs offer a broad formulation of the fitting process behind tarbiya.
terra: Determining and guiding set creation on a directed course, a non-bodily parallel to growth toward its proper limit.

luna: The section describes mercy as tenderness toward the weak; this ayah rebukes the opposite conduct, failing to honor an orphan. | terra: Failure to honor the orphan is an indictment of a society that treats inherited plenty without the mercy it owes its weak members.
luna: The section says care should become concrete help for the vulnerable; this ayah rebukes failing to urge the feeding of the needy.

luna: The section says mercy is tenderness that becomes help for the weak; this ayah names feeding on a day of hunger as a hard moral passage. | terra: Feeding on a day of hunger makes provision a difficult act, sharpening the section's household-food association.

luna: The section links a shared womb to kinship and care; this ayah names an orphan who is a near relative as a recipient of food. | terra: The hungry person singled out is an orphan of near relationship, where kinship and weakness coincide.
luna: The section directs tenderness toward the vulnerable; this ayah names a needy person in severe hardship as a recipient of food.

luna: The section's root raḥmah means tenderness that leads to good; this ayah calls believers to urge one another to patience and mercy (مَرْحَمَة). | terra: The hard path includes urging one another to patience and “مَرْحَمَة”; compassion is a practiced communal obligation.

luna: The section's home shelters a child who depends on another's care; this ayah says Allah found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter. | terra: God finds the addressee an orphan and gives shelter, a compact image of divine rearing before the later command concerning orphans.

luna: The section's image joins care with provision; this ayah says Allah found the Prophet in need and made him self-sufficient. | terra: Finding the addressee in need and enriching him pairs shelter with the household provision developed in the section.

luna: The section says mercy is directed especially to the weak; this ayah turns the Prophet's experience of orphanhood into the command not to oppress an orphan. | terra: The one who was sheltered as an orphan must not oppress an orphan; received care becomes care for the vulnerable.
luna: The section defines mercy as tenderness that becomes good action; this ayah commands not to repel the one who asks.
terra: The first command to read is in the name of the creating Rabb, joining lordship, creation, and instruction.
terra: Humanity is created from a clinging form; learning is announced beside an early formative state.
terra: The repeated command to read calls the teacher “your Rabb, the Most Generous,” giving generosity to the formative Lord.

luna: The section describes the teacher who nourishes people with small sciences; this ayah says the Lord taught by the pen, giving learning a concrete means. | terra: Teaching by the pen gives a concrete means by which nurture reaches knowledge.

luna: The section describes bringing a learner from one state toward completion; this ayah says Allah taught the human what he did not know. | terra: God teaches the human what he did not know, completing the movement from dependent origin to learned speech.
luna: The section defines mercy as active good toward the vulnerable; this ayah condemns the denier of judgment, whose conduct is specified in the following verses.

luna: The section calls for care of the weak; this ayah describes the opposite conduct, harshly repelling the orphan. | terra: Repulsing the orphan is named as a sign of denying judgment, the contrary of mercy that acts toward the weak.

luna: The section says mercy becomes concrete help; this ayah condemns failing to urge food for the needy. | terra: Alongside 107:2's orphan, failure to urge feeding the poor shows how rejection of the vulnerable includes withholding nourishment.
